games.explanation: The market is charging you a full underdog price on a team that's basically a coin flip once you actually look at the lineups. Soto against right-handed pitching is the best hitter in this game not named Judge, posting a .463 xwOBA on that side, and the Mets get to run him out in a park that plays neutral for runs but juices the ball over the fence. Yankee Stadium's short porch is a feature, not a bug, when your three-hole hitter barrels everything in sight. Getting +158 on a game our sim has landing inside a run is the kind of price that only exists because the pinstripes are on the other side of the ticket.

Bradish's line looks like an ace's until you notice who he's actually been getting out, and it isn't left-handed hitters. Lefties have tagged him for a .306 xwOBA with a walk rate north of twelve percent, which is a problem when Toronto rolls out a lineup that tilts left and stacks Guerrero, who's been punishing right-handed pitching all year. The sim spits out a dead-even projected score, which means a pick'em price on the better team by a comfortable Elo margin is doing the work for you. At -110, you're getting the Jays as a coin flip in a game they should be favored in.

Kumar Rocker is still figuring out how to get left-handed hitters out, and Arizona happens to trot out a lineup full of them. Marte, Perdomo, and Nootbaar are exactly the profile that has been feasting on this arm all year, with lefties tagging Rocker for a .391 xwOBA while he walks more than a batter an inning's worth of trouble. Pfaadt isn't an ace, but he doesn't need to be when the other guy is handing out free passes in a closed-roof park that neutralizes the one thing Texas hits well. -140 on the better team with the better matchup is the board catching up slowly, and we're not waiting around for it.

Seattle at this price assumes Bryan Woo turns every lineup he sees into the same problem, and the Athletics happen to be built to give him the wrong one. Woo has been quietly more mortal against lefties, and the A's roll out McNeil and Butler exactly where that split matters most. The sim has this as a one-run game, which is what happens when a division underdog is closer to a coin flip than a 43% team, and the market is still charging tourist rates on the favorite. +150 on a game the board should be pricing near even is the whole ballgame.

The market is pricing a laugher; the game on paper is a coin flip with a lead change or two. Take the cushion.

Phillips isn't a name, but he throws enough strikes to keep this a normal baseball game, and the sim lands on a one-run affair that looks nothing like the blowout the board is selling.
